questions.stem: A 58-year-old client recently widowed, who lives alone and owns a handgun, comes to the clinic for insomnia. While the nurse takes vital signs, the client says, "Things would be easier for everyone if I weren't around." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?"
"Your family would be devastated if anything happened to you."
"Let's get your sleep sorted out first, and then we can talk."
"Grief is hard. Most people feel that way for a while."

rationale.correct: Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plan, means and intent. Risk factors: older age, recent loss, living alone, access to a firearm.

perOption.a: Asking directly about suicide does not increase risk and is essential; this client has several risk factors.
perOption.b: This induces guilt and skips assessment.
perOption.c: Delaying assessment of a suicide cue is unsafe.
perOption.d: This minimizes the statement.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old was admitted with severe depression 12 days ago and started sertraline on admission. The client used to stay in bed but now attends groups, is eating and says, "I have more energy now." Mood is still low. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.text: The client's suicide risk may be higher now than on admission
The client is recovering and can move to less frequent observation
The medicine is not working and the dose needs to be raised
The client's risk is low because the client is taking part in groups

rationale.correct: Monitor closely as energy improves and in the early weeks of treatment, especially in young people.

perOption.a: Energy often returns before mood lifts, which can give the client the energy to act on a plan; young adults on antidepressants need close watching.
perOption.b: Improved energy with low mood is a high-risk period.
perOption.c: Antidepressants take 2 to 6 weeks for full effect on mood.
perOption.d: Participation does not rule out suicidal intent.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize periods of increased suicide risk.

questions.stem: A client is admitted to the psychiatric unit after a suicide attempt by hanging. The client says, "I'll find a way next time." Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Remove belts, shoelaces, cords and other items that could be used as a ligature
Start continuous one-to-one observation within arm's length
Search the client's belongings and the room for hazards
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts at regular intervals
Have the client sign a no-suicide contract instead of observation
Assign a private room at the end of the hall for privacy

rationale.correct: Suicide precautions: remove means, close observation, frequent assessment.

perOption.a: This removes the means.
perOption.b: Close observation prevents self-harm.
perOption.c: This reduces access to means.
perOption.d: Ongoing assessment is needed.
perOption.e: Contracts do not replace safety measures.
perOption.f: The client should be near staff.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with severe depression who has barely spoken for a week is suddenly calm and smiling, has given a favorite watch to a roommate and asks the nurse to mail letters to family members. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: The client may have decided on a suicide plan
The antidepressant has reached its full effect
The client is getting ready for discharge next week
The client is making friends on the unit

rationale.correct: Warning signs: sudden calm, giving things away, saying goodbye, putting affairs in order.

perOption.a: Sudden calm, giving away belongings and saying goodbye are warning signs.
perOption.b: Sudden improvement with these behaviors is a warning sign.
perOption.c: Goodbye letters and giving away belongings need assessment.
perOption.d: Giving away prized possessions is a warning sign.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the shift notes on a client admitted for depression 4 days ago. Highlight the statements or behaviors that are suicide warning signs.

segments.text: "I won't be a burden to anyone much longer."
asked a visitor to take the dog to a neighbor
. During a room check, staff found
several saved-up pills in a sock
ate half of breakfast and lunch
"I'm looking forward to my daughter's visit next week."

rationale.correct: Identify verbal, behavioral and situational warning signs of suicide.

perOption.s2: Talking about being a burden is a warning sign.
perOption.s4: Giving away pets or possessions is a warning sign.
perOption.s8: Poor appetite is common in depression but is not a suicide warning sign.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize suicide warning signs in documentation.

questions.stem: A client with severe depression has eaten less than a quarter of meals for 5 days, drinks little, has not bathed and stays in bed. The client denies suicidal thoughts and has no plan. The client has lost 3 kg. Which need comes first after safety is confirmed?

options.text: Nutrition and fluid intake
Bathing and personal hygiene
Getting the client to attend group therapy
Planning for discharge and outpatient care

rationale.correct: Depression: safety first, then physiological needs (nutrition, sleep), then self-care and therapy.

perOption.a: Physiological needs come next after safety.
perOption.b: This matters but ranks after nutrition and fluids.
perOption.c: This is lower priority.
perOption.d: This is lower priority.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with depression that has not responded to three antidepressants is scheduled for the first of a series of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) treatments. The client asks what to expect. What should the nurse tell the client?

options.text: "You may be confused and forget things for a while afterward."
"You'll be awake but relaxed, and you may feel the seizure."
"Have a light breakfast that morning so you have energy."
"Most people need just one treatment to get lasting relief."

rationale.correct: ECT: informed consent, NPO, anesthesia and muscle relaxant; monitor for confusion and memory changes.

perOption.a: Short-term confusion and memory loss are common and usually temporary.
perOption.b: General anesthesia and a muscle relaxant are used.
perOption.c: The client is NPO before the procedure.
perOption.d: A series of 6 to 12 treatments is usual.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in acute mania paces the halls, will not sit for more than a minute or two and has lost 4 kg since admission. The client drinks water but leaves meal trays untouched. What should the nurse offer?

options.text: Sandwiches and fruit the client can eat while walking
A full hot meal at a table in the busy dining room
A low-calorie diet with three small meals a day
No food until the client agrees to sit for a meal

rationale.correct: Mania: finger foods, fluids, reduced stimulation and rest periods.

perOption.a: Portable, high-calorie foods meet high energy needs.
perOption.b: The client cannot sit, and the dining room is overstimulating.
perOption.c: This does not meet high energy needs.
perOption.d: This risks malnutrition.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with bipolar disorder in a manic episode is talking loudly, telling jokes about other clients and taking over a card game in the dayroom. Other clients are getting angry. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Walk the client to a quieter area and set clear limits
Suggest the client lead a competitive group game
Explain to the client in detail why the jokes are hurtful
Let the other clients tell the client how they feel

rationale.correct: Mania: low stimulation, consistent limits, simple activities and safety.

perOption.a: Lower stimulation and firm, consistent limits help control behavior.
perOption.b: Competition increases stimulation.
perOption.c: Long explanations are lost on a client with racing thoughts.
perOption.d: This can escalate into conflict.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia sits in a corner with the head tilted, mumbling, and then says to the nurse, "The voices are telling me I'm bad and I deserve to be punished." What is the best response?

options.text: "I don't hear them. They sound scary. What are they telling you to do?"
"There are no voices. It's your illness talking to you."
"Tell me what the voices sound like. Are they male or female?"
"Try to ignore them, and they'll fade when your medicine starts working."

rationale.correct: Hallucinations: acknowledge the experience, present reality and assess content and safety.

perOption.a: This presents reality without arguing and assesses for command hallucinations.
perOption.b: Arguing damages trust.
perOption.c: This focuses on details that reinforce the hallucination rather than safety.
perOption.d: This dismisses the experience and misses safety.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia admitted last night says the voices have been getting louder for a week since the client stopped taking risperidone. The client looks frightened. What is the most important thing for the nurse to find out?

options.text: Whether the voices tell the client to harm self or others
Why the client stopped taking the risperidone last week
How many different voices the client is hearing
Whether the client has a family member to call

rationale.correct: Always assess for command hallucinations.

perOption.a: Command hallucinations are a safety risk.
perOption.b: Adherence matters, but safety comes first.
perOption.c: This does not affect immediate safety.
perOption.d: This is less urgent.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with schizophrenia approaches the nurse in a hospital gown and says, "I'm the chief surgeon here, and I need to get to the operating room for my first case." What is the best response?

options.text: "Being important seems to matter to you. Let's walk to the dayroom."
"You're not a surgeon. You're a patient on the psychiatric unit."
"Which operation are you planning to perform this morning?"
"I'll call the operating room to see whether they're ready for you now."

rationale.correct: Delusions: do not argue or agree; focus on feelings and reality.

perOption.a: This avoids arguing, responds to the feeling and redirects to reality.
perOption.b: Direct confrontation increases defensiveness.
perOption.c: This reinforces the delusion.
perOption.d: This agrees with and reinforces the delusion.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the admission assessment of a 22-year-old with a first episode of schizophrenia. For each finding, indicate whether it is a positive or negative symptom.

rows.text: Hears a voice commenting on what the client does
Face shows little expression during the interview
Believes neighbors put a camera in the ceiling
Has stopped going to class or seeing friends
Jumps between unrelated topics when answering
Answers in one or two words

rationale.correct: Positive symptoms add (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization); negative symptoms take away (flat affect, avolition, alogia, anhedonia).

perOption.r1:c1: Hallucinations add an experience, so they are positive symptoms.
perOption.r1:c2: Negative symptoms are losses of normal function.
perOption.r2:c1: This is not an added experience.
perOption.r2:c2: Reduced emotional expression (flat affect) is a negative symptom.
perOption.r3:c2: This is not a loss of function.
perOption.r4:c1: This is not an added experience.
perOption.r4:c2: Avolition and social withdrawal are negative symptoms.
perOption.r5:c1: Disorganized speech is a positive symptom.
perOption.r5:c2: This is not a loss of function.
perOption.r6:c1: This is not an added experience.
perOption.r6:c2: Poverty of speech (alogia) is a negative symptom.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with paranoid schizophrenia has refused all hospital meals for 2 days, saying the kitchen staff are poisoning the food. The client drinks only from sealed water bottles. What should the nurse offer?

options.text: Sealed, prepackaged foods the client can open
A nasogastric tube feeding to prevent malnutrition
A taste of each food by the nurse to show it is safe
A plan to withhold privileges until the client eats

rationale.correct: Paranoia: build trust, be consistent and use sealed foods.

perOption.a: Sealed packaging reduces suspicion and supports nutrition.
perOption.b: This is coercive and not warranted yet.
perOption.c: This can feed the delusion and does not build trust.
perOption.d: This is punitive.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder tells the day nurse, "You're the only one who understands me. The night nurses are cruel." The client asks to have only this nurse assigned. Night staff report the client said the same about them. What should the team do?

options.text: Agree on consistent rules and talk often as a team
Assign the day nurse to the client on as many shifts as possible
Have the day nurse tell the client the night nurses are kind
Transfer the client to another unit with a new team

rationale.correct: Borderline personality disorder: splitting, impulsivity and self-harm; use consistent limits, team communication and DBT.

perOption.a: Consistency across all staff counters splitting.
perOption.b: This reinforces splitting.
perOption.c: Defending staff can draw the nurse into the split.
perOption.d: Splitting will continue with any team.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with antisocial personality disorder tells a new nurse, "You're so much smarter than the others. You'd let me have my phone after 9 p.m., wouldn't you?" Unit rules collect phones at 9 p.m. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Restate the rule and collect the phone at 9 p.m.
Let the client keep the phone tonight to build rapport
Tell the client the rule is unfair but must be followed
Avoid the client for the rest of the shift

rationale.correct: Antisocial personality: manipulation; use firm limits and consistent consequences.

perOption.a: Clear, consistent limits reduce manipulation.
perOption.b: This rewards manipulation.
perOption.c: This undermines the team and the rules.
perOption.d: Consistent engagement with limits is better.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with anorexia nervosa is admitted with a BMI of 14.5. The heart rate is 42/min, blood pressure falls from 94/60 to 76/48 mm Hg on standing, potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and phosphorus is 2.4 mg/dL. Which action is the priority?

options.text: Begin cardiac monitoring and correct the electrolytes
Start a high-calorie diet to restore weight quickly
Explore how the client sees their body
Arrange a family therapy session this week

rationale.correct: Anorexia: medical stabilization first (cardiac, electrolytes), then slow refeeding and psychotherapy.

perOption.a: Bradycardia and hypokalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias; stabilization comes first.
perOption.b: Rapid refeeding risks refeeding syndrome, especially with low phosphorus.
perOption.c: This comes after medical stabilization.
perOption.d: This is important later.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with anorexia nervosa in an inpatient program has been medically stabilized and is gaining weight slowly. Staff notice napkins left on the tray and the client spending time in the bathroom after meals. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Supervise meals and observe the client for 1 hour after
Let the client eat alone in the room to reduce stress
Let the client weigh themself each morning in the room
Talk with the client about calories in each food choice

rationale.correct: Anorexia: supervised meals, blind weights done consistently and focus on feelings.

perOption.a: This prevents hiding food and purging.
perOption.b: This allows hiding food.
perOption.c: Weights are done by staff on a schedule, often blind.
perOption.d: The focus is on feelings rather than food details.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student at a normal weight comes to the clinic for fatigue. The student says, "Sometimes I eat a lot and feel out of control." Which other findings would most suggest bulimia nervosa?

options.text: Swollen cheeks and calluses on the knuckles
A BMI of 15 and fine, soft hair on the arms
A potassium of 5.6 mEq/L and peaked T waves
Weight gain of 10 kg over the past year

rationale.correct: Bulimia: binge-purge cycles, often normal weight, parotid swelling, dental erosion, hypokalemia.

perOption.a: Parotid swelling and Russell sign come from repeated self-induced vomiting.
perOption.b: Severe low weight and lanugo are more typical of anorexia.
perOption.c: Vomiting causes low potassium.
perOption.d: People with bulimia are often at a normal, stable weight.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who was denied an off-unit pass is pacing in the hallway, clenching both fists and shouting, "This place is a prison!" Other clients are moving away. The client has not hit anyone. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and offer choices
Call for a show of force and prepare restraints
Stand close and place a hand on the client's arm to calm them
Tell the client to calm down or the pass will be taken away for a week

rationale.correct: De-escalation: calm voice, safe distance, offer choices, reduce stimulation.

perOption.a: Verbal de-escalation is the first-line response to rising agitation.
perOption.b: Restraint is a last resort when de-escalation fails.
perOption.c: Touch and closeness may be seen as a threat.
perOption.d: Threats escalate the situation.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: At 1400, a client who punched a staff member was placed in seclusion in an emergency by the charge nurse. The client is now yelling but not hitting the walls. Which action is required?

options.text: Observe continuously; a provider must see the client within 1 hour
Check on the client every 2 hours until the next shift
Keep the client in seclusion until the yelling has stopped for 4 hours
Obtain a PRN seclusion order for future episodes

rationale.correct: Seclusion and restraint: last resort, time-limited orders, continuous monitoring, release as soon as safe.

perOption.a: Seclusion requires ongoing monitoring, a face-to-face evaluation within 1 hour and documentation.
perOption.b: Continuous monitoring is required.
perOption.c: Release happens as soon as the client is safe, not as a consequence.
perOption.d: PRN orders for seclusion are not allowed.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A new graduate nurse is orienting to an inpatient psychiatric unit and asks the preceptor what "milieu therapy" means. Which description should the preceptor give?

options.text: A safe, structured unit where clients take part in community life
Clients rest in their rooms for most of the day to reduce stimulation
A unit with few rules so that clients can practice freedom
Staff make the unit decisions so clients can focus on getting well

rationale.correct: Milieu therapy: structure, safety, community involvement and client responsibility.

perOption.a: The milieu uses the environment and community as part of treatment.
perOption.b: Isolation is not therapeutic.
perOption.c: Structure provides safety.
perOption.d: Client participation is encouraged.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
